experiments.title: Which queue is fastest for SPSC handoff?
experiments.question: One producer hands one small message (256 bytes) to one consumer, many times. Which in-process queue is fastest in each language?

story.why: Most services start with one writer and one reader in the same process.
story.example: A request thread puts work on a queue; a worker thread takes it.
story.tradeoff: A lock around a deque is simple. A lock-free or async channel may be faster, but only if the extra machinery is cheaper than the lock.

experiments.title: Does payload size change the ranking?
experiments.question: Same SPSC handoff as experiment 1, but the payload is a 4 KiB document instead of a 256-byte message. Does the ranking stay the same?

story.why: A ranking on tiny messages can hide copy cost that only shows up on bigger payloads.
story.example: A worker queue that moves whole HTTP bodies, not 256-byte tickets.
story.tradeoff: If the ranking flips, the “fastest queue” from experiment 1 is not a general answer.

experiments.title: Does ranking change under 1P4C, 4P1C, and 4P4C?
experiments.question: Same small message, but one producer and four consumers, four producers and one consumer, then four of each. Does the SPSC ranking still hold?

story.why: Real services rarely have exactly one writer and one reader.
story.example: Several request threads put work; a pool of workers take it.
story.tradeoff: A lock that looked cheap at 1P1C can convoy under many producers.

experiments.title: What happens when the queue is bounded and the consumer is slower?
experiments.question: The queue holds at most 32 messages. Consumers wait 5 microseconds per item. How do enqueue time and handoff change?

story.why: A bounded queue is backpressure. Unbounded queues hide overload until memory is gone.
story.example: A worker cannot keep up; producers must wait instead of filling RAM.
story.tradeoff: Blocking on full is a feature, not a failure.

experiments.title: How long does an empty-queue consumer take to wake?
experiments.question: The consumer waits on an empty queue. The producer sleeps, then puts one item. How long until the consumer has the item?

story.why: Handoff time when the queue is already full of work is not the same as wakeup cost.
story.example: A worker parks until the next request arrives.
story.tradeoff: A condition variable sleeps the core; a spin loop burns it.

experiments.title: How fast can a queue absorb a burst and then drain?
experiments.question: The producer dumps 1000 small messages as fast as it can, then the consumer drains. What is fill time and drain time?

story.why: Traffic is often a spike, not a steady trickle.
story.example: A fan-in of events after a deploy.
story.tradeoff: A huge burst needs either a large bound or fast drain.

experiments.title: How does an async queue behave with many waiting consumers?
experiments.question: One producer, 32 waiting async consumers, small messages. What is handoff time?

story.why: Event loops can have thousands of parked tasks. That is not the same as two threads.
story.example: An asyncio service with many waiters on one queue.
story.tradeoff: A library that is fast with two tasks can crawl with 32 waiters.

experiments.title: Does a bounded async queue apply backpressure?
experiments.question: An async queue with maxsize 32 and a slow consumer. Do producers wait instead of growing memory?

story.why: Async backpressure uses the event loop, not an OS mutex.
story.example: An async worker is slow; producers must await put().
story.tradeoff: The same bound as threads, different waiter.

experiments.title: How fast can waiting async consumers be cancelled?
experiments.question: Many tasks wait on an empty async queue. Cancel them all. How long does teardown take, and is the queue still sound?

story.why: Cancelled waiters are a common source of leaks and double-gets.
story.example: A request times out while its worker is parked on get().
story.tradeoff: Fast cancel that loses or doubles a message is not a win.

experiments.title: What does a cross-process queue cost versus in-process?
experiments.question: Python multiprocessing.Queue moves the same 256-byte message. How does handoff compare to queue.Queue?

story.why: The GIL pushes some work into processes. Serialization is part of that number.
story.example: A parent process hands jobs to worker processes.
story.tradeoff: IPC is a different category. Do not plot it next to deque-lock.

experiments.title: Does a shared-memory ring beat pickle IPC on a small payload?
experiments.question: A mapped SPSC ring versus multiprocessing.Queue for a 256-byte message.

story.why: Shared memory skips pickle of the body. That only matters if the copy path is the cost.
story.example: Two processes share a ring of bytes.

experiments.title: What does local durability cost versus an in-memory queue?
experiments.question: A SQLite-backed queue with fsync off, then on. How much slower is a durable put/get than queue.Queue?

story.why: Disk and fsync dominate. This is not a lock benchmark.
story.tradeoff: Never rank this next to a deque.
